questions.question: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion with one example each.
questions.solution:
**Nuclear fission:** A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy.
Example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + energy (used in nuclear reactors)

**Nuclear fusion:** Two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
Example: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + energy (powers the sun and hydrogen bombs)
questions.knowledgeNote: Fission requires critical mass; fusion requires extremely high temperature (~10⁷ K). Fusion releases more energy per kg than fission.
questions.answer: **Nuclear fission:** a **heavy nucleus splits** into two (or more) lighter nuclei plus neutrons, releasing energy because the fragments have higher binding energy per nucleon — *example:* **²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV** (chain reaction in reactors and weapons). **Nuclear fusion:** **two light nuclei merge** into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy because the product again has higher binding energy per nucleon — *example:* **²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV** (the Sun's energy source; requires enormous temperature/pressure to overcome Coulomb repulsion). **Differences:** (1) fission breaks a heavy nucleus, fusion builds a light one; (2) fission needs slow-neutron capture and is chain-reactive; fusion needs extreme temperature to force like charges together; (3) both release energy *because both move products toward the iron peak* of binding energy per nucleon. **Deep point:** the energy arrow points the same way for both — toward higher binding energy per nucleon — which is why fission burns uranium downhill from the peak and fusion burns hydrogen uphill toward it.
